title: EV Charger Installation Cost Guide: What Glasgow Homeowners Actually Pay
metaTitle: EV Charger Installation Cost Guide (Glasgow) | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What does a home EV charger really cost in Glasgow? A clear breakdown of typical prices, what's included, and what pushes the cost up.
excerpt: A clear breakdown of what a home EV charger actually costs, what's included in the price, and the three things most likely to push yours higher.
keyTakeaways: A standard 7kW home charger install typically costs somewhere between £800 and £1,200, all in
The charger unit and the labour are usually similar in cost — it's rarely one expensive part and one cheap part
Cable run length, consumer unit condition, and parking setup are the three things that most often push the price up
Smart charging capability has been a legal requirement for new home chargers since 2022
intro: "How much does an EV charger actually cost?" is the question we get asked more than almost any other — usually from someone who's just picked up their first electric car and wants a straight answer before they commit to anything.
The honest answer is that it depends on your property, but there's a real, predictable range most Glasgow homes fall into. Here's what actually drives that number.

sections.heading: The typical price range
body: For a standard 7kW smart home charger — the setup most homeowners end up with — you're usually looking at somewhere between £800 and £1,200 including the unit and installation. That figure covers a straightforward install: a domestic supply that can take the extra load, a reasonably short cable run from your consumer unit to where the charger's going, and no groundworks.

It's rarely a case of a cheap charger and expensive labour, or vice versa — the two costs tend to land in a similar bracket, which is why the total moves as a block rather than one part staying fixed while the other swings.

sections.heading: What's actually included
body: A proper quote for a home EV charger should include the charger unit itself, all fixings and mounting, the cable run from your consumer unit, a check of your existing electrical supply to confirm it can handle the extra load, and full testing and certification once it's fitted.
list: The charger unit and wall mounting bracket
Cabling from your consumer unit to the charge point
A load assessment of your existing supply
Earthing arrangement appropriate to your property (PME or a dedicated earth rod where needed)

sections.heading: What pushes the cost up
body: Three things account for almost every quote that comes in above the standard range.
list: Cable run length — a charger fitted right next to your consumer unit is cheaper than one routed to a detached garage or the far side of a driveway
Consumer unit condition — if your board is old, undersized, or doesn't have the right protection, it may need upgrading alongside the charger (see our consumer unit upgrade guide below)
Parking setup — chargers for on-street parking or shared driveways sometimes need extra groundworks or a different mounting approach than a standard private driveway install

sections.heading: Smart chargers aren't optional anymore
body: Since 2022, all new home and workplace EV chargers installed in Great Britain are legally required to have smart charging capability — meaning they can be scheduled and monitored remotely, and default to off-peak charging times. This isn't an upsell; every charger we fit meets this requirement as standard.

sections.heading: How long does the job actually take?
body: For a standard domestic install, most jobs are done within half a day. Longer cable runs, or any consumer unit work identified during the survey, will extend that — which is exactly why we always survey before quoting, rather than pricing blind over the phone.

faqs.q: Can I get a grant for a home EV charger?
faqs.a: Homeowners with a private driveway are generally no longer eligible for a home charger grant. If you rely on on-street parking, a cross-pavement solution grant may still be available — we can point you in the right direction during your survey.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission?
faqs.a: Almost never for a standard home installation. It's only a consideration for certain listed buildings or conservation area restrictions.

faqs.q: Will my consumer unit need upgrading too?
faqs.a: Sometimes — it depends on the age and capacity of your existing board. We check this as part of every EV charger survey, so there are no surprises once work starts.

faqs.q: How long does installation take on the day?
faqs.a: Most home installs are completed within half a day.

title: 7 Signs Your Glasgow Home Needs Rewired
metaTitle: 7 Signs Your House Needs Rewired | Quality Electrics Glasgow
metaDescription: Flickering lights, warm sockets, an old fuse box — here are the 7 real warning signs that your Glasgow home's wiring needs attention.
excerpt: Flickering lights and a trip now and again could be nothing — or they could be your wiring telling you something. Here's what to actually look for.
keyTakeaways: Most wiring has a useful life of around 25–30 years — plenty of Glasgow's tenement stock is well past that
An old fuse box with wire fuses (rather than modern circuit breakers) is one of the clearest signs on its own
Burning smells or scorch marks around sockets are not a 'wait and see' issue
An EICR is the only way to know for certain whether you need a full rewire or just remedial work
intro: Glasgow's housing stock is a mix of Victorian tenements, 1930s semis, post-war schemes, and new-builds — and a good chunk of it is carrying wiring that's older than the people living in it. Rewiring is a significant job, so it's worth knowing the difference between a minor niggle and a genuine warning sign before you call anyone out.

sections.heading: 1–2. Flickering lights and frequent trips
body: An occasional flicker when a big appliance kicks in isn't automatically a problem. But lights that flicker regularly across multiple rooms, or a consumer unit that trips more than very occasionally, usually points to a deeper issue — loose connections, overloaded circuits, or wiring that's simply reached the end of its working life.

sections.heading: 3. Warm sockets, buzzing, or a burning smell
body: This is the one sign that shouldn't wait for a convenient time. A socket or switch that feels warm to the touch, a buzzing or crackling sound behind a wall, or any smell of burning around an outlet means you should stop using that circuit and get it looked at as a priority, not schedule it in for next month.

sections.heading: 4. Scorch marks around sockets or switches
body: Brown or black marks around a socket or switch plate are a visible record of overheating that's already happened — not a risk that might happen. If you see this, treat it the same way as a burning smell.

sections.heading: 5. An old fuse box with rewireable wire fuses
body: If your consumer unit still uses physical fuse wire rather than modern circuit breakers, that's usually a strong sign the wider installation is overdue an update — this style of fuse box was largely phased out decades ago and lacks the RCD protection built into every modern board.

sections.heading: 6. Round-pin sockets or fabric-sheathed cable
body: Round-pin sockets, or wiring with a fabric or rubber outer sheath rather than modern PVC, are clear indicators of a pre-1970s installation. If you can see either of these anywhere in the property, it's a strong prompt to get the whole installation assessed.

sections.heading: 7. The property simply hasn't been rewired in 25–30 years
body: Even with no obvious symptoms, wiring has a working life — generally reckoned at around 25 to 30 years. If nobody in living memory of the property can tell you when it was last rewired, age alone is a good enough reason to get it checked.

sections.heading: How to actually find out
body: None of the above tells you for certain whether you need a full rewire, a partial rewire, or nothing more than a repair. The only way to know is an Electrical Installation Condition Report (EICR) — see our full landlord and homeowner guide to EICRs below.

faqs.q: Does every old fuse box mean I need a rewire?
faqs.a: Not necessarily — sometimes just the consumer unit needs upgrading while the cabling itself is still sound. An EICR will tell you which applies to your property.

faqs.q: How long does a full rewire take?
faqs.a: A typical two or three-bedroom tenement flat takes around a week, though we'll confirm an exact timeline once we've surveyed the property.

faqs.q: Can a rewire be done in stages?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly for occupied homes or businesses that can't close entirely — we can scope a phased approach at quote stage.

faqs.q: Is rewiring covered by any certification?
faqs.a: Yes, every rewire we carry out is tested to BS7671 and certified on completion.

title: EICR for Landlords in Scotland: The Complete 5-Year Rule Explained
metaTitle: EICR for Landlords in Scotland: Legal Requirements Explained
metaDescription: What Scottish landlords legally need to know about EICR frequency, tenant notification, and what happens if a property fails.
excerpt: Scottish landlords have a specific legal duty around EICRs that's stricter than a lot of guidance online suggests. Here's what the law actually requires.
keyTakeaways: Scottish landlords are legally required to hold a valid EICR for every rented property, at least every 5 years
The EICR must be carried out by an electrician accredited with SELECT or NICEIC
A copy must go to the tenant within 28 days of the inspection
If a report identifies a serious risk, remedial work isn't optional — it's part of meeting the Repairing Standard
intro: If you let property in Scotland, your electrical safety obligations are set out clearly in law — this isn't a grey area or a 'best practice' recommendation, it's a legal requirement under the Housing (Scotland) Act 2006 and the Repairing Standard. Here's what that actually means in practice.

sections.heading: How often do you actually need one?
body: At minimum, every 5 years, or sooner if a previous report specifically recommends a shorter interval, or at a change of tenancy if the existing report is close to expiry. If your electrician flags the wiring as old or in poor condition and recommends more frequent checks, that recommendation should be followed rather than treated as optional.

sections.heading: Who can actually carry one out
body: An EICR for a Scottish rental property must be carried out by a qualified electrician accredited with SELECT (Scotland's own electrotechnical trade association) or NICEIC. A report from an unaccredited contractor doesn't meet the Repairing Standard, regardless of how thorough it looks.

sections.heading: What the report needs to cover
body: A compliant EICR isn't just a look at the consumer unit — it needs to include an appliance check (PAT) covering anything you as the landlord provide, alongside the full inspection and testing of the fixed electrical installation.

sections.heading: Getting it to your tenant
body: Once the inspection's complete, you're required to provide a copy of the EICR to your tenant within 28 days. This isn't just good practice — it's part of the legal obligation, so it's worth building into your process rather than treating as an afterthought.

sections.heading: What happens if the property fails
body: A failed EICR isn't the end of the road, but it does mean action is required. Issues are coded by severity, and anything coded as a serious risk needs to be remedied to bring the property up to the Repairing Standard. We list every issue found, rated by severity, and can quote for remedial work on the spot — so you're not left waiting on a second contractor to even get a price.

faqs.q: Do I need an EICR for every rented property I own?
faqs.a: Yes, each individual rented property needs its own valid, in-date EICR.

faqs.q: What if I've just had a full rewire done?
faqs.a: A rewire comes with its own Electrical Installation Certificate, which satisfies the requirement until your next scheduled EICR is due.

faqs.q: How long does an inspection take?
faqs.a: A typical flat or house takes 2–4 hours on site; larger properties take longer, which we'll scope in advance.

faqs.q: Do I get the report the same day?
faqs.a: You'll get a verbal summary on the day, with the full written report following shortly after.

faqs.q: Is this different from an EPC?
faqs.a: Yes — an EPC covers energy efficiency, an EICR covers electrical safety. They're separate legal requirements.

title: Consumer Unit Upgrade Cost Guide: Fuse Box vs Modern Board
metaTitle: Consumer Unit Upgrade Cost Guide | Quality Electrics Glasgow
metaDescription: What does a consumer unit upgrade cost, what's included, and when is it worth doing? A straight-talking guide for Glasgow homeowners.
excerpt: Still running an old fuse box? Here's what a modern consumer unit actually costs, what you get for it, and when it's genuinely worth doing.
keyTakeaways: A standard dual-RCD consumer unit typically costs £500–£800; a full RCBO board is usually £800–£1,200
It's not a legal requirement to upgrade an old fuse box — but modern boards include safety protection old ones simply don't have
You can't legally do this yourself — it requires a qualified electrician and Part P notification
Most upgrades are completed within half a day to a full day
intro: "Fuse box" and "consumer unit" get used interchangeably, but if yours is genuinely an old fuse box — with fuse wire or fuse cartridges rather than switches — it's worth understanding exactly what upgrading it involves, and what it actually costs.

sections.heading: What you're actually paying for
body: A standard dual-RCD consumer unit typically runs £500–£800 all in; stepping up to a full RCBO board — where every circuit gets its own individual protection rather than sharing an RCD between several — is usually £800–£1,200. The higher spec isn't just an upsell: individual RCBO protection means a fault on one circuit doesn't knock out every other circuit sharing that RCD.
list: Removal and safe disposal of the old fuse box or consumer unit
Supply and installation of the new unit
Testing of every circuit it feeds

sections.heading: What can add to the cost
body: A few things commonly sit outside the base price and are worth asking about upfront: earth bonding upgrades (often £150–£300 if your property's earthing needs updating to match the new board), minor plaster repair around the unit if it's being relocated, and remedial work if testing uncovers a fault on an existing circuit.

sections.heading: Is it actually a legal requirement?
body: No — you're not legally required to replace a working fuse box. But older units generally lack RCD protection, which is what actually cuts power fast enough to prevent a serious electric shock. If yours is flagged during an EICR, or you're adding a new heavy load like an EV charger, that's usually the point it becomes worth doing rather than putting off.

sections.heading: Why you can't do this yourself
body: Consumer unit replacement is notifiable work under Part P of the Building Regulations, and it needs to be carried out and certified by a qualified, registered electrician — not something to attempt as a weekend project, regardless of how it looks online.

faqs.q: How long does an upgrade take?
faqs.a: Most homes are done in half a day to a full day, depending on how many circuits need re-terminating.

faqs.q: Will the power be off the whole time?
faqs.a: Yes, temporarily — we agree a time that suits you and keep the power-down window as short as possible.

faqs.q: Do I need a new consumer unit if mine fails an EICR?
faqs.a: If it's marked as a serious risk (C1/C2), yes — we can quote for the upgrade at the same visit as the inspection.

faqs.q: What size unit do I need?
faqs.a: It depends on your existing circuits and anything you're planning to add, like an EV charger — we work this out during a free survey.

title: How Much Can Your Business Save by Upgrading to LED Lighting?
metaTitle: Commercial LED Lighting Savings Guide | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: Real energy and maintenance savings from switching a commercial unit to LED lighting, and how long it typically takes to pay back.
excerpt: LED isn't just a bulb swap — it's usually one of the fastest-paying-back upgrades a commercial property can make. Here's the real numbers.
keyTakeaways: LED can cut the lighting portion of a commercial energy bill by 50–75%
Typical payback periods run 2–5 years, with some fit-outs paying back in as little as 12 months
Maintenance costs also drop sharply — LEDs last roughly five times longer than fluorescent tubes
Financing routes like Salix loans and Enhanced Capital Allowances can improve the numbers further
intro: For a lot of commercial clients, lighting is the easiest energy cost to fix and the one most often left until something actually fails. The numbers involved usually make a stronger case than most other efficiency upgrades available to a small or mid-sized business.

sections.heading: The energy savings, in real terms
body: Switching from fluorescent or older lighting to LED typically cuts the lighting portion of an energy bill by 50–75%. For a warehouse or retail unit running high-bay or tube fixtures for long hours, that difference shows up on the bill immediately — one documented UK warehouse case saw 200 high-bay fixtures switched to LED, cutting annual lighting energy costs from roughly £14,000 to £4,900.

sections.heading: How fast does it pay for itself?
body: Typical payback periods sit between 2 and 5 years, with well-scoped fit-outs sometimes paying back in as little as 12 months, particularly where lighting runs long hours (retail, warehousing, hospitality). After payback, the running-cost saving is effectively pure benefit for the rest of the fixtures' working life.

sections.heading: Maintenance costs drop too
body: LED fixtures last around 50,000 hours on average — roughly five times longer than fluorescent tubes — which means far fewer call-outs to replace failed tubes and starters. Maintenance cost reductions of 60–80% after an LED upgrade aren't unusual, particularly for properties with hard-to-access fittings like high ceilings or stairwells.

sections.heading: Financing the upgrade
body: A full LED fit-out doesn't have to be paid upfront. Salix Finance offers interest-free loans for qualifying energy-efficient equipment including LED lighting, and Enhanced Capital Allowances can allow 100% first-year tax relief on qualifying products — both worth discussing with your accountant alongside a quote.

sections.heading: Getting it right the first time
body: A good LED fit-out isn't just swapping fittings one-for-one — lux levels, glare, and emergency lighting compliance all need to be part of the design, not an afterthought. We scope this properly before quoting, and can work around your trading hours so the switch doesn't cost you in downtime what it saves you in energy.

faqs.q: Can the work be done outside our trading hours?
faqs.a: Yes — evening, overnight, or phased installs around opening hours are common for retail and office fit-outs.

faqs.q: Do you handle emergency lighting as part of the upgrade?
faqs.a: Yes, including testing and certification to keep you compliant.

faqs.q: Is LED suitable for every type of commercial space?
faqs.a: In almost all cases yes, though the fixture spec differs — a retail unit, warehouse, and office each need a different lighting design, not the same fitting everywhere.

faqs.q: Do you offer ongoing maintenance after the fit-out?
faqs.a: Yes, maintenance contracts are available so you've got a fixed point of contact rather than calling around for every issue.

title: Electrical First Fix Checklist: What to Plan Before Your Extension or Loft Conversion
metaTitle: Electrical Checklist for Extensions & Loft Conversions | QE
metaDescription: What actually needs planning at first fix stage for a home extension or loft conversion, and why it matters before plastering starts.
excerpt: First fix is the point of no return before plastering — get it wrong and you're chasing out fresh walls. Here's what to plan in advance.
keyTakeaways: First fix happens before plastering — cables, back boxes, and wiring routes are locked in at this stage
Loft conversions have specific requirements around mains-wired smoke alarms and extractor fan wiring
Electrical work on an extension must comply with Part P of the Building Regulations
A registered electrician can self-certify the work, avoiding a separate building control inspection
intro: Once plastering starts on your extension or loft conversion, changing your mind about where a socket or light switch goes gets expensive fast. First fix is the stage where all of that gets decided — so it's worth planning properly before the electrician is even on site, not during.

sections.heading: What actually happens at first fix
body: First fix covers everything that needs to go in before the walls are closed up: cables run through joists and studwork, back boxes fitted for sockets and switches, and wiring routed for lighting, heating controls, alarms, and anything else electrical the room needs.
list: Cable runs through walls, floors, and ceilings
Back boxes for sockets, switches, and dimmers
Wiring for lighting circuits, including any feature or under-unit lighting
Data, TV aerial, and smart home cabling — much cheaper to include now than retrofit later

sections.heading: Loft conversions have their own rules
body: Building regulations are specific about loft conversions: mains-wired smoke alarms are required, with defined locations, and any extractor fan (for an en-suite, for example) needs to be wired in at first fix — not bolted on afterwards. Power points and lighting also need agreeing before plasterboard goes up, since retrofitting later means cutting into a finished ceiling.

sections.heading: Why timing with your builder matters
body: The single biggest cause of extra cost on extension electrics is being brought in too late — after first fix should have already happened. Ideally we're involved as soon as first fix is being scheduled, working directly from your architect's drawings or discussing the layout with your builder, so nothing gets missed and nothing needs re-cutting.

sections.heading: Certification and building control
body: Electrical work on an extension has to comply with Part P of the Building Regulations. Using a registered electrician (through NICEIC, for example) means the work can be self-certified, which saves you arranging a separate building control inspection for the electrics specifically. At the end of the job you should receive an Electrical Installation Certificate, a Building Control notification certificate, and full test results — keep all three with your property paperwork.

faqs.q: When should I bring an electrician in on the project?
faqs.a: As early as possible — ideally once first fix is being scheduled with your builder, so sockets, lighting, and circuits are positioned correctly the first time.

faqs.q: Do you work directly from architect drawings?
faqs.a: Yes, and we're comfortable coordinating on-site with the rest of your build team rather than working in isolation.

faqs.q: Is Building Standards certification included?
faqs.a: Yes, we certify the electrical work to the standard your local authority requires.

faqs.q: Can you wire outbuildings and garden rooms as part of the same job?
faqs.a: Yes, including outdoor supplies and garden offices alongside the main extension or conversion.

title: Kitchen Renovation Electrics: What to Plan Before Your Fitter Arrives
metaTitle: Kitchen Renovation Electrics Guide | Quality Electrics Glasgow
metaDescription: Socket placement rules, dedicated circuits, and what to agree with your electrician before your kitchen fitter starts work.
excerpt: Get the electrics agreed before your kitchen fitter starts, not during — here's exactly what needs planning and why.
keyTakeaways: Sockets must sit at least 300mm from a sink and at least 450mm above the floor under UK regulations
Ovens, hobs, and large appliances usually need their own dedicated circuit, not a shared socket circuit
All new kitchen wiring must be RCD protected
Getting the layout agreed before units go in avoids expensive retrofitting later
intro: A kitchen carries more electrical load, in a smaller space, than any other room in the house — which is exactly why it's the room most likely to go wrong if the electrics aren't planned before the units arrive.

sections.heading: Socket placement rules
body: There are clear regulations behind where kitchen sockets can go, not just design preference: sockets need to sit at least 300mm (horizontal distance) from the edge of a sink to reduce water risk, and at least 450mm above the floor under UK building regulations. A common practical placement is around 150mm above the worktop, or 100mm above an upstand — high enough to be usable, low enough not to look like an afterthought.

sections.heading: Circuits: what needs its own
body: General kitchen worktop sockets usually run off a ring final circuit or a 20A radial circuit. But bigger appliances typically need their own dedicated circuit rather than sharing: an electric oven or hob commonly needs a 32A or 40A radial circuit of its own, and it's good practice to give a dishwasher, washing machine, and any American-style fridge-freezer their own circuits too, rather than loading them onto the general sockets.

sections.heading: RCD protection is non-negotiable
body: Under current building regulations, all new kitchen wiring must be RCD protected — this isn't a nice-to-have given how much water and how many appliances share the space, it's a requirement, and it should be built into your consumer unit setup rather than treated as optional.

sections.heading: Timing with your kitchen fitter
body: The order of operations matters: electrics need to be agreed and largely first-fixed before your kitchen units go in, not worked around afterwards. That means the socket layout, lighting positions, and any dedicated circuits should be settled with your electrician while you're still finalising the kitchen design — ideally with your fitter or designer in the conversation too, so nobody's plans conflict once work starts.

sections.heading: Don't forget the lighting
body: Under-cabinet and feature lighting is easy to leave as an afterthought and hard to add cleanly once units are fitted. If you want it, it needs wiring in at first fix, with cable routed to sit invisibly behind cabinetry rather than run externally after the fact.

faqs.q: When should I book an electrician relative to my kitchen fitter?
faqs.a: Before the units go in, ideally at first-fix stage, so sockets and circuits land in the right places once cabinets are fitted.

faqs.q: Do induction hobs need a dedicated circuit?
faqs.a: Yes, almost always — we size the circuit to the specific hob being installed.

faqs.q: Can you work directly with my kitchen designer or fitter?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly work from kitchen design plans and coordinate directly with the fitter.

faqs.q: How long does a kitchen electrical first and second fix take?
faqs.a: Typically 1–2 days combined, depending on the size of the kitchen and how much lighting is involved.

title: What Is an EICR? A Plain-English Guide
metaTitle: What Is an EICR? Plain-English Guide | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What an EICR actually checks, who needs one, and what the different fault codes mean — explained without the jargon.
excerpt: EICR gets thrown around a lot without much explanation. Here's what the report actually checks, who legally needs one, and what those C1/C2/C3 codes on the results mean.
keyTakeaways: An EICR is a formal inspection of a property's fixed electrical installation, not the appliances plugged into it
It results in a report classified as satisfactory or unsatisfactory, with any issues coded by severity
Scottish landlords have a legal duty to hold a satisfactory EICR, renewed at least every five years
A domestic inspection typically takes a few hours and doesn't usually require major disruption
intro: EICR is one of those terms that gets mentioned constantly around property, mortgages, and renting, but rarely gets properly explained. It stands for Electrical Installation Condition Report, and it's essentially a formal health check for the fixed wiring in a building.
Here's what it actually involves, what the results mean, and when you genuinely need one.

sections.heading: What actually gets inspected
body: An EICR looks at the fixed parts of a property's electrical installation — the wiring itself, the consumer unit, sockets, switches, and earthing and bonding arrangements. It's not checking your appliances or anything plugged in; that's what PAT testing covers separately.

The inspection combines a visual check with a series of electrical tests: earth continuity, insulation resistance, and how quickly protective devices like RCDs actually trip. It's a proper diagnostic process, not a walk-round with a torch.

sections.heading: What the report classifications mean
body: The finished report is classified as either satisfactory or unsatisfactory, and any issues found are coded by severity. A C1 means danger present, requiring immediate action. A C2 means potentially dangerous, requiring urgent remedial work. A C3 is an improvement recommended, but not a safety failure in itself. FI simply means further investigation is needed to reach a conclusion on a specific point.
Only C1 and C2 codes make a report unsatisfactory overall — a report with only C3 observations can still be classified satisfactory, which surprises a lot of people expecting a strict pass or fail.

sections.heading: Who actually needs one
body: Landlords letting residential property in Scotland have a clear legal duty to hold a satisfactory EICR, generally renewed at least every five years. Homeowners aren't legally required to have one, but it's commonly requested by mortgage lenders, insurers, and buyers during a property sale.

sections.heading: How long it actually takes
body: For a typical domestic property, an inspection usually takes a few hours on-site, with the written report following within a couple of working days. It's not usually disruptive — the electrician isolates circuits briefly for testing rather than cutting power for extended periods.

faqs.q: How is an EICR different from a PAT test?
faqs.a: An EICR checks the fixed wiring and installation of a property. PAT testing checks portable appliances plugged into it. They cover different things and neither replaces the other.

faqs.q: What happens if my EICR comes back unsatisfactory?
faqs.a: You'll get a clear breakdown of what's been coded C1 or C2 and why, along with a quote for the remedial work needed to bring it back to a satisfactory standard.

faqs.q: Can I get an EICR done quickly if I need one urgently?
faqs.a: Often yes, particularly for a single domestic property — get in touch and we'll do our best to fit you in around a tight deadline.

faqs.q: Is an EICR the same as a Building Warrant?
faqs.a: No — an EICR is a condition report on existing wiring, while a Building Warrant relates to approval for new building work. They're separate processes.

title: What Is an RCD and Why Does It Matter?
metaTitle: What Is an RCD? How It Protects Your Home | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What an RCD actually does, how it's different from a fuse, and how to tell if your consumer unit has proper RCD protection.
excerpt: RCD gets mentioned on every electrical report but rarely explained. Here's what it actually does, how it differs from a fuse, and why it's the single biggest safety upgrade in most older homes.
keyTakeaways: An RCD detects tiny imbalances in current and cuts power fast enough to prevent a fatal shock
It's a different kind of protection to a fuse or MCB, which respond to overload and short circuits, not shock risk
Many older fuse boxes have no RCD protection at all, or only cover some circuits
Modern consumer units fit RCD protection — usually via RCBOs — on every circuit individually
intro: RCD stands for Residual Current Device, and it's arguably the single most important piece of safety equipment in a modern consumer unit — yet most people couldn't explain what it actually does if asked.
Here's the plain version, and how to check whether your home actually has it.

sections.heading: What an RCD actually detects
body: An RCD constantly monitors the current flowing out through the live wire against the current flowing back through the neutral. In a healthy circuit, those two figures match. If some current is leaking to earth — through a person, water, or damaged cable — there's an imbalance, and the RCD detects it.

When it detects a leak above a set threshold, typically 30mA for personal protection, it disconnects the circuit in under 40 milliseconds. That speed is what makes the difference between a shock and a fatal one.

sections.heading: How this is different from a fuse or MCB
body: A standard fuse or MCB (miniature circuit breaker) protects against overload and short circuits — too much current flowing through the wire itself, which risks fire. It has no way of detecting current leaking to earth through a person, which is a completely different failure mode.
That's why a property can have fuses or MCBs that work perfectly and still offer no protection against electric shock — the two systems are solving different problems.

sections.heading: How to tell if your home has RCD protection
body: Open your consumer unit and look for a device labelled RCD, or individual breakers labelled RCBO — these combine both overload and RCD protection in one unit per circuit. If you see only rows of plain MCBs, or worse, an old fuse box with rewireable fuses, there's likely no RCD protection at all.

sections.heading: Why older homes are often missing it
body: RCD protection wasn't a standard requirement for most circuits until relatively recently in UK wiring regulations. Plenty of homes with wiring that's otherwise sound simply predate the requirement — which is usually the actual reason an older consumer unit gets flagged on an inspection, rather than the wiring itself being faulty.

faqs.q: Can I add an RCD without a full consumer unit upgrade?
faqs.a: Sometimes a single RCD module can be added, but a full upgrade to individual RCBOs per circuit is usually the better long-term fix, since one circuit tripping won't take out the whole board.

faqs.q: Why does my RCD trip when I plug something in?
faqs.a: Usually a faulty appliance leaking current, or occasionally a damp outdoor connection. It's doing its job — worth getting the specific cause diagnosed rather than just resetting it repeatedly.

faqs.q: Is one RCD enough for the whole house?
faqs.a: It's better than nothing, but if it trips, everything on that RCD loses power at once. Individual RCBOs per circuit mean only the affected circuit trips.

faqs.q: Do I need RCD protection to sell my house?
faqs.a: It's not a strict legal requirement to sell, but it's frequently flagged on surveys and EICRs, and buyers increasingly expect it.

title: How Long Does an EICR Last?
metaTitle: How Long Does an EICR Last? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: How long an EICR stays valid for homeowners, landlords, and commercial premises in Scotland, and what actually triggers an earlier renewal.
excerpt: The honest answer depends on who owns the property and what it's used for. Here's the actual timeline for homeowners, landlords, and commercial premises.
keyTakeaways: For rented residential property in Scotland, an EICR is generally valid for five years
Commercial premises and older installations are often recommended a shorter interval
There's no fixed legal expiry for owner-occupied homes, though it's still good practice to renew periodically
Certain events — like a failed report or major electrical work — can trigger the need for a fresh EICR earlier
intro: "How long does an EICR last?" is one of the most common follow-up questions we get after explaining what one actually is, and the honest answer depends on what the property's used for.
Here's the breakdown by property type, plus the situations that can force a renewal earlier than expected.

sections.heading: Rented residential property
body: For private rented housing in Scotland, the standard interval is five years, or sooner if the previous report recommends it. Landlords have a legal duty to keep a satisfactory report in place continuously — not just get one done once and forget about it.

sections.heading: Owner-occupied homes
body: There's no fixed legal expiry for a homeowner's own EICR, since there's no statutory duty to have one at all. That said, most electricians recommend renewing every ten years for a standard domestic property, or five years if the property is older or the last inspection flagged concerns worth monitoring.

sections.heading: Commercial and industrial premises
body: Commercial properties are often recommended shorter intervals — frequently five years, sometimes less depending on the type of premises and how the electrical installation is used. Higher-risk environments, like those with heavy machinery or public access, often warrant more frequent inspection regardless of any specific legal minimum.

sections.heading: What can trigger an earlier renewal
body: A change of tenancy, a failed or unsatisfactory previous report, significant electrical work being carried out, or simply a specific recommendation on the last EICR for an earlier re-check can all mean a fresh inspection is needed before the standard interval is up.

faqs.q: Does the five-year clock reset after remedial work?
faqs.a: Remedial work fixes the specific issues found — a fresh EICR (or at minimum a minor works certificate for the fix) confirms the property's now satisfactory, and the renewal clock generally runs from that inspection.

faqs.q: What happens if my landlord EICR lapses?
faqs.a: You'd be in breach of the legal duty to hold a satisfactory report — worth booking a renewal well before the expiry date rather than after it's lapsed.

faqs.q: Do I need a new EICR every time I get a new tenant?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, provided your existing EICR is still within its valid period and remains satisfactory — but it's worth checking the exact date rather than assuming.

faqs.q: Can you remind me before my EICR is due for renewal?
faqs.a: Yes — we can set up a renewal reminder so it's a scheduled visit rather than a scramble against a deadline.

title: What Is Surge Protection, and Do You Actually Need It?
metaTitle: What Is Surge Protection? Do You Need It? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What a surge protection device (SPD) actually does, what causes power surges, and whether your home genuinely needs one fitted.
excerpt: Surge protection gets offered on almost every consumer unit quote now. Here's what it actually protects against, and how to judge whether it's worth it for your home.
keyTakeaways: A surge protection device (SPD) guards against sudden voltage spikes reaching your home's electronics
Surges can come from lightning strikes, the grid itself, or even large appliances switching off nearby
UK wiring regulations now require an SPD risk assessment on new and upgraded consumer units
It's a one-off fit into the consumer unit, not something added per appliance
intro: Surge protection has gone from a rarely-mentioned extra to something offered on nearly every consumer unit upgrade quote, and understandably, people want to know whether it's a genuine necessity or an upsell.
Here's what it does, and how the current regulations actually treat it.

sections.heading: What a power surge actually is
body: A power surge is a brief, sudden spike in voltage above the normal supply level. It can come from a lightning strike near the property, switching events on the wider electricity grid, or even large appliances and motors switching off elsewhere in the building, which can send a brief spike back through shared wiring.

These spikes are usually far too brief to trip a breaker, but they can be more than enough to damage sensitive electronics — think TVs, boilers with electronic controls, and anything with a circuit board.

sections.heading: What a surge protection device does
body: A surge protection device (SPD) sits in the consumer unit and diverts excess voltage safely to earth before it can reach the circuits feeding your sockets and appliances. It's a single component fitted once, rather than something you'd need on every individual plug.

sections.heading: Is it actually required?
body: Current UK wiring regulations require an SPD risk assessment whenever a consumer unit is installed or upgraded, weighing factors like the consequences of a surge (data loss, safety systems, etc.) against the likelihood of one occurring. In many cases, particularly properties with a lot of connected electronics or in areas more exposed to lightning activity, that assessment concludes an SPD is genuinely warranted, not just a nice-to-have.

sections.heading: What it doesn't cover
body: An SPD protects against external and grid-related surges, not a direct lightning strike on the property itself, and it doesn't replace good practice like unplugging genuinely sensitive equipment during severe storms. It's one solid layer of protection, not a total guarantee.

faqs.q: Can surge protection be added without a full consumer unit upgrade?
faqs.a: In some cases yes, if there's suitable space in the existing unit — we'll assess this and let you know honestly whether it's straightforward or whether a fuller upgrade makes more sense.

faqs.q: Does surge protection stop appliances breaking from everyday use?
faqs.a: No — that's general wear and tear, not what an SPD is designed for. It specifically addresses voltage spikes, not mechanical or age-related failure.

faqs.q: Is surge protection worth it for a small flat?
faqs.a: It depends on the risk assessment for that specific property — we'll give you an honest answer rather than a blanket yes, based on what's actually connected and the supply situation.

faqs.q: How much does adding an SPD typically cost?
faqs.a: It's a relatively small addition compared to the rest of a consumer unit upgrade — we'll quote it clearly alongside the main job so you can see it as a separate line item.

title: What Is an RCBO? RCD vs RCBO Explained
metaTitle: What Is an RCBO? RCD vs RCBO Explained | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What an RCBO actually is, how it combines RCD and MCB protection, and why modern consumer units use one per circuit.
excerpt: RCBO is one of the more confusing acronyms in home electrics — mostly because it's doing the job of two older devices at once. Here's what it means in practice.
keyTakeaways: An RCBO combines the functions of an RCD (shock protection) and an MCB (overload protection) in a single device
Modern consumer units typically fit one RCBO per circuit, rather than sharing an RCD across several
This means a fault on one circuit trips only that circuit, not several at once
RCBOs are more expensive per circuit than a shared RCD setup, but offer better fault isolation
intro: RCBO is one of those acronyms that shows up on a quote and rarely gets unpacked properly, mostly because it's really two other acronyms combined into one device — RCD and MCB.
Here's what it actually means, and why it's become the standard for modern consumer units.

sections.heading: Breaking down what it combines
body: RCBO stands for Residual Current Breaker with Overcurrent protection. It combines what an MCB does — protecting against overload and short-circuit current that could cause a fire — with what an RCD does — detecting current leaking to earth that could cause an electric shock. One device, two jobs.

sections.heading: Why this matters compared to an older setup
body: Older consumer units often used a single shared RCD covering several circuits at once, alongside separate individual MCBs. The problem with that setup is that a fault on any one of those circuits trips the shared RCD, which takes out every circuit connected to it — lights, sockets, and everything else on that side of the board goes off together.

With an RCBO fitted per circuit, a fault on your kitchen sockets trips only the kitchen sockets. The rest of the property, including the lights, stays on. It's a genuinely practical improvement, not just a technical upgrade.

sections.heading: Why not every consumer unit has always used them
body: Cost is the main reason — RCBOs are individually more expensive than plain MCBs paired with a shared RCD, so older installations, especially in properties fitted out before RCBOs became the practical standard, often used the cheaper shared arrangement instead.

sections.heading: What this means for a consumer unit upgrade
body: When we upgrade an older board, moving to individual RCBOs per circuit is standard practice now, not an optional extra — it's a meaningfully better setup for very little extra cost once you're already replacing the whole unit.

faqs.q: Do I need to replace my whole consumer unit to get RCBOs?
faqs.a: In almost all cases yes, since RCBOs need to be fitted into a compatible board — it's not usually something added to an old unit piecemeal.

faqs.q: Are RCBOs more likely to trip than a shared RCD?
faqs.a: No — they're just as reliable, they simply isolate the specific circuit at fault rather than taking the rest of the board down with it.

faqs.q: Is RCBO protection a legal requirement?
faqs.a: It's not a blanket legal requirement for every home, but it's what current wiring regulations expect for new consumer unit installations.

faqs.q: Can I mix RCBOs and standard MCBs in the same board?
faqs.a: Yes, this is common, particularly if only some circuits need individual protection — we'll advise honestly on what your specific property needs.

title: How Much Does an EICR Cost in Glasgow?
metaTitle: How Much Does an EICR Cost in Glasgow? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: A clear breakdown of what an EICR typically costs for a flat, house, or commercial unit in Glasgow, and what actually affects the price.
excerpt: The honest range for an EICR depends more on property size and circuit count than most people expect. Here's what actually drives the price.
keyTakeaways: EICR pricing typically starts from around £200 excl. VAT for a standard flat, scaling up with property size and circuit count
Number of circuits, not floor area alone, is the main driver of cost
Commercial EICRs are priced separately, based on the size and complexity of the installation
A genuinely clear quote should specify what's included before you book, not just a flat headline figure
intro: EICR pricing varies more than people expect, and the honest reason isn't inconsistent electricians — it's that the number of circuits in a property, not just its size, is what actually determines how long the inspection takes.
Here's a realistic breakdown of what drives the cost.

sections.heading: Typical starting price
body: For a standard flat or smaller property, EICR pricing typically starts from around £200 excluding VAT. Larger homes with more circuits, more bedrooms, and more sockets and fixed appliances will cost more, since there's simply more to test.

sections.heading: What actually drives the price up
body: Circuit count is the biggest factor — a property with a straightforward single consumer unit and a handful of circuits is quicker to test than one with an extension, outbuilding, or multiple consumer units feeding different parts of the property. Access difficulty and the age of the installation also play a role, since older or poorly documented wiring can take longer to test and interpret properly.

sections.heading: Commercial EICR pricing
body: Commercial and industrial premises are priced individually rather than against a standard domestic range, since the size and complexity of installations varies hugely — from a single small retail unit to a multi-circuit warehouse. We'll always survey or discuss the property properly before quoting rather than guessing from a generic price list.

sections.heading: What should be included in the price
body: A proper EICR quote should include the full inspection and testing, the written report itself, and a clear explanation of any findings — not just the site visit with the report as a costly add-on. Ask directly what's included before booking if a quote doesn't make this clear.

faqs.q: Is the EICR report itself extra on top of the inspection?
faqs.a: No, with us the written report is included as standard in the quoted price, not billed separately afterwards.

faqs.q: Does an unsatisfactory result cost extra to fix?
faqs.a: Any remedial work needed is quoted separately and clearly, so you know exactly what you're agreeing to before anything further is booked.

faqs.q: Is a landlord EICR priced differently to a homeowner's?
faqs.a: The inspection itself is the same process — pricing is driven by property size and circuit count, not who owns it.

faqs.q: Can you give me a fixed price before you've seen the property?
faqs.a: For straightforward standard properties, often yes over the phone — for anything larger or unusual, we'll confirm with a quick look first so the quote's accurate.

title: How Much Does Rewiring a House Cost in Glasgow?
metaTitle: House Rewiring Cost Guide (Glasgow) | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: A realistic breakdown of full and partial rewire costs for Glasgow homes, and the property factors that actually move the price.
excerpt: A full rewire quote can vary a lot between properties, and it's rarely about the electrician — it's the property itself driving the number. Here's what actually matters.
keyTakeaways: A full rewire cost is driven mainly by property size, number of circuits, and how accessible the walls and floors are
Tenement flats and period properties often cost more per room than modern new-builds
A partial rewire, targeting only affected circuits, is sometimes genuinely enough and considerably cheaper
Making good after chasing walls is a real cost to factor in, separate from the electrical work itself
intro: "How much will it cost to rewire my house?" doesn't have a single answer, and anyone quoting one figure over the phone without seeing the property is guessing. What actually drives the price is a combination of size, access, and property type.
Here's a realistic breakdown of what moves the number up or down.

sections.heading: The main cost drivers
body: Property size and the number of circuits involved is the single biggest factor — more rooms means more sockets, switches, and light positions to rewire, which is straightforwardly more materials and labour. Beyond that, access matters just as much: a property with easy underfloor and loft access is faster to chase cable through than one with solid floors and lath-and-plaster walls throughout.

sections.heading: Why tenement and period properties often cost more
body: Glasgow's tenement flats and period homes bring genuine complications a modern new-build simply doesn't have — solid stone or lath-and-plaster walls that are harder to chase cleanly, shared stairwells and common areas that sometimes need factor involvement, and older layouts that don't always follow a predictable cable route. None of this makes a rewire impossible, but it does typically push the cost and timeline up compared to an equivalent-sized modern property.

sections.heading: Full rewire vs partial rewire
body: A full rewire replaces every circuit in the property. A partial rewire targets only the circuits that are actually faulty, undersized, or unsafe, leaving sound existing wiring untouched. It's considerably cheaper where it's genuinely appropriate — the honest answer depends on what an inspection actually finds, not a blanket assumption either way.

sections.heading: Making good — a cost that's easy to forget
body: Chasing cable into walls means those channels need filling and making good afterwards. We include basic making good as standard, but a full plaster skim across affected walls is typically a separate cost, usually handled by a plasterer — factor this into your overall budget, not just the electrical quote.

faqs.q: Can you give me an accurate quote without visiting the property?
faqs.a: Not accurately for a full or partial rewire — there are too many variables specific to your property. We'll always survey before quoting properly.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to rewire an empty property?
faqs.a: Often yes, since access is easier without furniture and belongings in the way, though it's not always practical to empty a property just for this reason.

faqs.q: Does a rewire include new sockets and switches, or just cabling?
faqs.a: A proper rewire quote includes the sockets, switches, and light fittings themselves, not just the cable behind the walls — worth confirming this is included in any quote you're comparing.

faqs.q: How do I know if I need a full rewire or just a partial one?
faqs.a: An inspection is the honest way to find out — we'll tell you plainly which your property actually needs rather than defaulting to the bigger job.

title: How Often Should a House Be Rewired?
metaTitle: How Often Should a House Be Rewired? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: The general rule of thumb for house rewiring intervals in the UK, and the practical signs that matter more than age alone.
excerpt: There's a commonly quoted rule of thumb for rewiring intervals, but the honest answer depends more on condition than a fixed number of years. Here's how to actually judge it.
keyTakeaways: The commonly quoted rule of thumb is a rewire roughly every 25 to 30 years
Condition, not just age, is what actually determines whether wiring needs replacing
An EICR is the reliable way to establish the actual state of a property's wiring, rather than guessing from age alone
Some older wiring still performs safely well past 30 years if it was well installed and hasn't been altered badly since
intro: There's a commonly repeated rule of thumb that a house should be rewired roughly every 25 to 30 years, and while it's a reasonable general guide, it's not a strict deadline — condition matters more than a number of years on a calendar.
Here's how to actually judge whether your home's wiring needs attention.

sections.heading: Where the 25-to-30-year guideline comes from
body: Cable insulation and general wiring components do degrade over time, and older materials used decades ago don't always match the standards and safety features expected today. The 25-to-30-year figure is a sensible average based on typical component lifespan and how wiring regulations have evolved over that period — but it's a guide, not a hard rule that applies identically to every property.

sections.heading: Why condition matters more than age alone
body: A well-installed system that's been left alone and properly maintained can genuinely still be sound at 30-plus years, while a poorly maintained or badly altered system can develop real issues well before that. What actually matters is the physical condition of the cabling, the presence (or absence) of RCD protection, and whether the installation has kept pace with the loads modern homes actually put on it.

sections.heading: The practical warning signs worth acting on
body: Regardless of the property's age, certain signs are worth taking seriously: frequent tripping, warm sockets or switches, flickering lights unrelated to a specific appliance, a persistent burning smell, or still having a fuse box with rewireable fuses rather than modern circuit breakers. Any of these are reasons to get an inspection regardless of what year the property was last rewired.

sections.heading: Why an EICR is the honest way to actually know
body: Rather than guessing from age, an EICR gives you an actual, evidenced answer on the condition of your wiring — tested and classified rather than assumed. It's the difference between a rule of thumb and a genuine diagnosis.

faqs.q: My house is 35 years old — does it definitely need rewiring?
faqs.a: Not necessarily — age alone doesn't tell the full story. An inspection will give you a genuine answer based on actual condition, not just the property's age.

faqs.q: Can a rewire be done in stages rather than all at once?
faqs.a: Yes, a partial or phased rewire targeting specific circuits or areas is often a practical option, particularly for a property that's still liveable but has specific concerns.

faqs.q: Does buying an older property mean I should assume a rewire is needed?
faqs.a: It's worth budgeting for the possibility, but get an EICR done rather than assuming — plenty of older properties have already been rewired or are still genuinely sound.

faqs.q: Will my insurance be affected by old wiring?
faqs.a: Some insurers do ask about the age and condition of wiring, and unresolved known issues can affect cover — worth being upfront and addressing anything flagged.

title: Do I Need an EICR to Sell My House?
metaTitle: Do I Need an EICR to Sell My House? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: Whether an EICR is legally required to sell a home in Scotland, and why buyers, solicitors, and lenders often ask for one anyway.
excerpt: There's no strict legal requirement, but in practice an EICR often ends up part of the sale anyway. Here's why, and when it's worth getting ahead of it.
keyTakeaways: There's no strict legal requirement for a homeowner to hold an EICR to sell their property
Buyers, solicitors, and mortgage lenders frequently request one during the sale process regardless
Getting one done proactively can prevent delays later in a sale, rather than scrambling once it's requested
An unsatisfactory report doesn't stop a sale, but it usually leads to a price or repair negotiation
intro: There's no law in Scotland that says a homeowner must hold a valid EICR to sell their property — but in practice, it comes up in a large number of sales anyway, usually requested by someone else in the chain rather than required upfront.
Here's who actually asks for one, and why it's often worth getting ahead of it.

sections.heading: The legal position
body: For owner-occupied property being sold, there's no statutory requirement to produce an EICR. This is different from the position for landlords letting a property, who do have a clear legal duty to hold one — the sale of a home you live in yourself isn't covered by the same rules.

sections.heading: Why it comes up anyway
body: Buyers' solicitors, surveyors, and sometimes mortgage lenders frequently ask for evidence of the electrical installation's condition as part of due diligence, particularly for older properties or where a survey has flagged the wiring as worth checking. It's not a legal box that must be ticked, but in a competitive market it can genuinely smooth or stall a sale depending on whether you already have an answer ready.

sections.heading: The case for getting one done before listing
body: Getting an EICR done proactively, before a buyer or their solicitor asks, means you're not scrambling to book an inspection and potential remedial work at a point in the sale where delays cost real money and goodwill. It also gives you an honest picture of anything worth fixing before it becomes a negotiating point.

sections.heading: What happens if the report comes back unsatisfactory
body: An unsatisfactory EICR doesn't stop a sale outright, but it typically leads to a conversation about who fixes what, or a price adjustment reflecting the cost of remedial work. Having the report — and ideally the remedial work already sorted — puts you in a stronger position than a buyer finding an issue themselves late in the process.

faqs.q: Will my sale definitely fall through without an EICR?
faqs.a: No, it's not a legal requirement to sell — but not having an answer ready if it's requested can cause delays at a sensitive point in the process.

faqs.q: How far in advance of listing should I get one done?
faqs.a: As early as feels practical — it gives you time to address anything found without it becoming a rushed, last-minute issue during a live sale.

faqs.q: Does the buyer usually pay for the EICR instead?
faqs.a: It varies by transaction and who requests it — there's no fixed rule, and it's often simply agreed between the parties or their solicitors.

faqs.q: Is an EICR the same thing a surveyor checks?
faqs.a: No — a standard survey may make general comments on visible wiring, but it isn't a substitute for a proper EICR, which involves actual testing.

title: What Is Part P Electrical, and When Does It Apply?
metaTitle: What Is Part P Electrical Work? | Quality Electrics
metaDescription: What Part P actually covers, which jobs count as notifiable electrical work in Scotland, and how self-certification works.
excerpt: Part P gets mentioned on quotes without much explanation. Here's what it actually covers, and why it matters for Scottish building regulations even though the name comes from England and Wales.
keyTakeaways: Part P is technically an England and Wales building regulation, but Scotland has its own equivalent notifiable work rules
Notifiable electrical work includes new circuits, consumer unit replacements, and work in bathrooms or other special locations
A registered electrician can self-certify notifiable work, avoiding a separate council application
Not all electrical work is notifiable — many repairs and additions to existing circuits fall outside these rules
intro: Part P comes up a lot in conversations about electrical work, though strictly speaking it's an England and Wales building regulation — Scotland has its own, broadly similar system under Scottish building regulations, which is what actually applies here.
Here's what the underlying idea covers, and what it means in practice for work done on a Scottish property.

sections.heading: What the regulation is actually trying to achieve
body: The core idea, whether under Part P in England and Wales or the equivalent Scottish building regulations, is that certain types of electrical work carry enough risk that they need to be properly certified as meeting current safety standards — not just completed, but formally signed off.

sections.heading: What counts as notifiable work in Scotland
body: New circuits, consumer unit replacements, and electrical work in special locations like bathrooms (where water and electricity are both present) are typical examples of notifiable work. Simpler jobs — like adding a socket to an existing circuit or replacing a like-for-like fitting — often fall outside these rules, though it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

sections.heading: How self-certification actually works
body: As a registered electrician with an approved certification scheme, we can self-certify notifiable work on your behalf. This means the job is properly certified as meeting Building Standards without you needing to apply for a separate building warrant through the council — the paperwork is handled as part of the job itself.

sections.heading: Why this matters if you're doing DIY or hiring unregistered work
body: Work carried out without proper certification — whether DIY or by someone not registered with an approved scheme — can cause real problems later, particularly when selling a property or making an insurance claim, since there's no formal proof the work meets current safety standards.

faqs.q: Do I need a building warrant for a new socket?
faqs.a: Generally no — adding a socket to an existing circuit typically isn't notifiable work, though we'll confirm this for your specific job.

faqs.q: Is bathroom electrical work always notifiable?
faqs.a: Often yes, given the water risk involved — we'll tell you clearly whether your specific bathroom job needs certification.

faqs.q: What proof do I get once notifiable work is certified?
faqs.a: You'll receive a certificate confirming the work meets current standards, which you should keep for future reference, insurance, or sale purposes.

faqs.q: Does self-certification cost extra?
faqs.a: It's built into the cost of notifiable work as standard with a registered electrician, not billed as a separate line item.
